items.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: And he played the Teddy Wilson, “Sweet Lorraine.” And I thought I wanted to play just like that. That’s my first introduction.

ctx.x: So I really wanted to touch piano, and you can imagine my parents all of a sudden they couldn’t buy a piano for me. So I took a job in a dance hall. And I think it was lucky for me, and for the Japanese people. And one of the Japanese young men, he’s not young anymore now, every once in a while, his name is Mr. Figree, and he was a jazz record © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

collector. And somehow he thought I had potentiality. So he invited me over to his home and played a traditional record. It’s a kind of famous story. And he played the Teddy Wilson, “Sweet Lorraine.” And I thought I wanted to play just like that. That’s my first introduction. It was in 1947 I believe.

items.title: Akiyoshi Toshiko — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: he played Teddy Wilson’s “Sweet Lorraine”—this became a very famous story. But when I heard him playing it, I said, “I want to play just like that!”

ctx.x: Of course. And there was a Hit Kit … you remember Hit Kit? I don‟t know.

[Army Navy] Hit Kit [of Popular Songs] is one of the things that the servicemen … every month or maybe twice a month, I‟m not quite sure, it was American hit songs. It was for the American servicemen. And you could get them, I think they had all those, you know, “Five Minutes More,” or like “Shoo Fly Pie,” what have you [laughs], things like that. It was lead sheets, that‟s what they played. I didn‟t know any chord symbols, I‟d never seen [those] in my life. So I said, “What‟s this?” So the violin player said,…
